name: Hawking-Turok Instanton
description: A deformed 4-sphere with no time in it, regular at one pole and singular at the other, on which a scalar field climbs its potential; Stephen Hawking and Neil Turok found it in 1998 for a generic potential. Cut through its poles and continued to real time, it holds an infinite open universe that inflates beside a timelike singularity, with no false vacuum.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The instanton and the two instantons in closed form are Riemannian, of signature $(+,+,+,+)$, and the region outside the bubble wall and the open universe are Lorentzian.
history: A deformed 4-sphere cut through its poles and continued into real time has, inside the light cone of one pole, an infinite open universe that inflates [hawking1998open]. Sidney Coleman and Frank De Luccia had found an open universe inside a bubble of lower vacuum energy, and Martin Bucher, Alfred Goldhaber, and Neil Turok built open inflation on it in 1995, with the inflaton stuck in a false vacuum until one bubble nucleates, then rolling slowly inside it [coleman1980, bucher1995]. Stephen Hawking and Turok, in Cambridge, built their open universe in February 1998 with no false vacuum, from the no-boundary proposal of James Hartle and Hawking, in which the Euclidean geometry is compact [hartle1983, hawking1998open]. With it, they wrote, "open inflation is generic and does not require any special properties of the inflaton potential" [hawking1998open].¶Their instanton is a space of four dimensions with no time, $ds^2 = d\sigma^2 + b^2(\sigma)\,d\Omega_3^2$, in which the radius $b$ of the 3-spheres of latitude is "a deformed version of the sine function" [hawking1998open]. A scalar field $\phi$ starts at $\phi_0$ at the regular pole $\sigma = 0$, where $b \approx \sigma$, and climbs its potential $V$ while $b$ grows, turns over, and is driven to zero at $\sigma_f$ as $(\sigma_f - \sigma)^{1/3}$, where $\phi$ diverges logarithmically [hawking1998open]. The Ricci scalar there grows as $\tfrac{2}{3}(\sigma_f - \sigma)^{-2}$ [turok1998four]. Since $V$ diverges there only logarithmically and the volume $b^3$ vanishes linearly, the Euclidean action $S_E = -\pi^2\int b^3 V\,d\sigma$ is finite, and there is one instanton for each $\phi_0$ [hawking1998open]. When $\phi'$ returns to zero exactly at $\sigma_f$, both poles are regular and the instanton is Coleman and De Luccia's [hawking1998open, lavrelashvili1998].¶With $d\Omega_3^2 = d\psi^2 + \sin^2\psi\,d\Omega_2^2$, the 3-surface $\psi = \pi/2$ through both poles has vanishing extrinsic curvature, and with $\psi = \pi/2 + i\tau$ the half sphere continues to a de Sitter-like region outside a null "bubble wall" that leaves the regular pole [hawking1998open]. Beyond the wall, with $\sigma = it$ and $\tau = i\pi/2 + \chi$, lies the open universe $ds^2 = -dt^2 + a^2(t)(d\chi^2 + \sinh^2\chi\,d\Omega_2^2)$ with $a(t) = -ib(it)$, and the singularity is a timelike world line that stays outside it [hawking1998open, turok1998four]. William G. Unruh drew the whole spacetime as a finite universe, part of it a homogeneous open one as large as one likes, closed off by a naked, timelike, attractive singularity [unruh1998]. Weighting each instanton by $e^{-2S_E}$ and asking that our galaxy formed, Hawking and Turok found the most probable open universe to have a density parameter today of $\Omega_0 \approx 0.01$, "too low to be compatible with current observations" [hawking1998open]. Andrei Linde replied that galaxies in such a universe would be $10^{10^8}$ light years apart, and that most models have $\Omega_0 = 1$ when the action enters with the opposite sign, as in the tunnelling wave function [linde1998open]. Hawking and Turok answered that reversing the sign leaves the fluctuations unsuppressed [hawking1998comment].¶Alexander Vilenkin built an instanton with the same singularity in flat space from a massless field, with $\phi' = -C/b^3$ and $b'^2 - 4\pi GC^2/3b^4 = 1$, and its continuation is a singular bubble growing at nearly the speed of light [vilenkin1998singular]. If such instantons are allowed, Vilenkin argued, flat space would by now be "overrun by expanding singular bubbles" [vilenkin1998singular]. Turok and Hawking answered that their singularity stays outside the open universe where observations are made, and that Vilenkin's expands to infinity [turok1998four]. Zhong Chao Wu pointed out that the action changes with $\phi_0$, and read each solution as a constrained instanton, stationary only with its 3-geometry fixed [wu1998]. Treating Vilenkin's instantons that way, Turok showed in 1999 that with the constraint imposed they have no negative mode, so flat space is stable [turok1999]. George Lavrelashvili found a negative mode about these instantons for some potentials with a false vacuum [lavrelashvili1998].¶Jaume Garriga found in 1998 that Vilenkin's instanton is the reduction to four dimensions of a smooth instanton of five dimensions, a cigar times a 3-sphere, in which the circle of the fifth dimension shrinks to zero at the singularity [garriga1998smooth]. Turok and Takeshi Chiba recognised it as the Euclidean Schwarzschild solution of five dimensions [turok1999, chiba1998]. Continued to real time it is a bubble of nothing that "eats up" space as it expands, and flat space with an extra dimension much larger than the Planck length decays through it slowly [garriga1998smooth]. With a cosmological constant in five dimensions the field has the potential $\lambda e^{2\kappa\phi/3}$ in four, with $\lambda$ a constant and $\kappa = (12\pi G)^{1/2}$, and an instanton of this kind is known in closed form, $ds^2 \propto \cos\chi\,(d\chi^2 + \sin^2\chi\,d\Omega_3^2)$, regular at $\chi = 0$ and singular at $\chi = \pi/2$ [garriga1998smooth, kirklin2001]. It is smooth in five dimensions for one value of $\phi_0$ alone, Garriga noted, so these instantons cannot produce a range of $\Omega_0$ [garriga1998smooth]. Kelley Kirklin, Turok, and Toby Wiseman read the singularity as a linear zero of the conformal factor on a regular space with the topology of $RP^4$, the 4-sphere with antipodal points identified [kirklin2001].¶Garriga, wrapping the singularity in a membrane, and Masashi Hashimoto, counting the bolt it becomes in five dimensions, found that it adds one third of the Gibbons-Hawking boundary term to the action [garriga2000singular, hashimoto2001]. Stephen Hawking and Harvey S. Reall found that such instantons from eleven dimensional supergravity on a squashed 7-manifold remain singular in eleven dimensions, with potentials too steep for inflation [hawking1998reall]. Steven Gratton and Turok found the fluctuations about the singular instantons fixed by the Euclidean action alone, with only modes that vanish at the singularity allowed [gratton1999], and with Thomas Hertog found them a better match to the COBE data on large angular scales than thin walled Coleman-De Luccia instantons [gratton2000observational]. Vilenkin, who called the instanton "a sphere with a thorn", granted that it had "invigorated the debate about the basic issues of quantum cosmology" [vilenkin1999debate]. Anton Chudaykin, Mikhail M. Ivanov, Renata Kallosh, Linde, Oliver H. E. Philcox, and Yusuke Yamada found in 2026 that a slightly open universe, with curvature parameter $\Omega_k \simeq 3 \times 10^{-3}$, fits cosmic microwave background and galaxy data better than a flat one, and set aside its creation from the instanton as "rather controversial" [chudaykin2026].

related.text: The instanton whose field comes to rest just as the second pole closes, so that both poles are regular; it needs a potential with a false vacuum [hawking1998open].
The instanton with its field at a stationary point of the potential, where the field never moves and the deformed 4-sphere is round [hawking1998open].
Inside the bubble wall is an open Friedmann universe, $k = -1$, with the scale factor $a(t) = -ib(it)$ continued from the instanton [hawking1998open].
Outside the bubble wall the continued instanton is "a spatially inhomogeneous De Sitter-like metric", and de Sitter space itself when the field stays constant [hawking1998open].
Riemannian solutions of Einstein's equations. This one has a scalar field and ends on a singularity, and its action is finite all the same [hawking1998open].
The same no-boundary proposal with the 4-sphere cut at its equator, where it continues to a closed universe [hawking1998open].

Kirklin, Turok, and Wiseman found the instanton to be conformal to a regular space with the topology of $RP^4$, the 4-sphere with antipodal points identified, with its singularity on a noncontractible $RP^3$ [kirklin2001].

coordinates.name: Instanton

parameters.description: Radius of the 3-sphere of latitude $\sigma$, a length, with $b \approx \sigma$ near the regular pole $\sigma = 0$ and $b \propto (\sigma_f - \sigma)^{1/3}$ near the singularity $\sigma = \sigma_f$. It is $\ell\sin(\sigma/\ell)$ on the round 4-sphere of radius $\ell$, where the field rests at a stationary point of its potential
Proper distance from the regular pole to the singularity, a length

coordinates.convention: We use the proper distance $\sigma$ from the regular pole, a length, and the angles $\psi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ on the 3-sphere of latitude $\sigma$. We leave $b(\sigma)$ free, a prime is a derivative with respect to $\sigma$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length.

coordinates.name: Outside the Bubble Wall

parameters.description: Radius of curvature of the hyperboloid at $\sigma$, a length, continued from the radius of the instanton's 3-sphere of latitude $\sigma$. It vanishes on the bubble wall $\sigma = 0$, where $b' = 1$, and at the singularity $\sigma = \sigma_f$
Proper distance from the bubble wall to the singularity, a length

coordinates.convention: We continue the instanton's chart with $\psi = \pi/2 + i\tau$, with $\tau$ a dimensionless time, itself the chart's $x^0$, $\sigma$ a length, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ the angles of the 2-sphere. We leave $b(\sigma)$ free, a prime is a derivative with respect to $\sigma$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Open Universe

parameters.description: Scale factor of the open universe, a length, zero on the bubble wall $t = 0$, where $a' = 1$, and continued from the radius $b$ of the instanton's 3-spheres as $a(t) = -ib(ict)$

coordinates.convention: We continue the chart outside the bubble wall with $\sigma = ict$ and $\tau = i\pi/2 + \chi$, with $t$ having dimensions of time, the proper time since the bubble wall along the comoving world lines, and $\chi$ a rapidity, a pure number. We leave the scale factor $a(t)$ free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Exponential Potential

parameters.description: Length setting the size of the instanton, with $\ell^2 = 3c^4/(4\pi GV_0)$ for the potential energy density $V_0$ of the field at the regular pole $\chi = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use the angle $\chi$ from the regular pole and the angles $\psi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ on the 3-sphere of latitude $\chi$, all pure numbers. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length.

coordinates.name: Vilenkin's Instanton

parameters.description: Length setting the size of the instanton, with $b = T^{1/2}(A^2 + T^2)^{1/4}$ the radius of its 3-sphere at $T$

coordinates.convention: We use Chiba's coordinate $T$, a length, zero at the singularity and the radius of the 3-spheres far from it, and the angles $\psi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ on those 3-spheres. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length.
